sents: I have good memories of my kindergarten in China, and of the stories our teacher told us there.
One of them I still remember is *The kitten who goes fishing*.
The kitten goes to the river with its mother.
Every time a dragonfly or a butterfly passes, it drops the rod and runs after it, while its mother sits by the water and catches fish after fish, until the kitten learns to sit still.
The teacher's lesson was that if you cannot stay with what you set out to do, you will achieve nothing.
It is a lesson for a lifetime, though many children forget it soon enough.
But it is not a lesson that AI has taken to heart, even though any model can tell you what the story means.
An LLM trained to do well at every reply is optimised the way the kitten is, one moment at a time, always going for what it is most likely to catch right then.
It works up to a point, since each reply catches something useful.
But the bucket stays empty.
In the Introduction chapter, I mentioned a case how AI and a human would handle a situation differently.
When sorting a customer complaint, and refering to how Bob did it, human asked Who's bob?

AI would start a crusde to find him, his employement record etc, while a human would simply he was quite a few years before you - all you need is he is not current - and proceed with the complaint handling, the goal at hand.
A frequent example: after an introduction at a meeting, the model drafted the follow-up email.
It wrote out our address, the road name and the year the mill was built, and never said why we wanted to meet.
Sometimes the butterfly is a puzzle.
A prospective customer replied to one of our emails, and the model noticed that the email gave two different numbers for the same thing.
It spent the rest of the session working out why, and the customer, who was the reason for the email, was forgotten.
Asked why, the model said the numbers did not match, so it checked them.
The first pillar is to play for the goal.

batches.assembled_prompt:
The intended reader has read the essay's introduction, which lists seven pillars, the behaviours an AI employee needs; this chapter is about the first of them.

The text, each paragraph starting with its number:

[P1] I have good memories of my kindergarten in China, and of the stories our teacher told us there. One of them I still remember is *The kitten who goes fishing*.

[P2] The kitten goes to the river with its mother. Every time a dragonfly or a butterfly passes, it drops the rod and runs after it, while its mother sits by the water and catches fish after fish, until the kitten learns to sit still. The teacher's lesson was that if you cannot stay with what you set out to do, you will achieve nothing.

[P3] It is a lesson for a lifetime, though many children forget it soon enough. But it is not a lesson that AI has taken to heart, even though any model can tell you what the story means. An LLM trained to do well at every reply is optimised the way the kitten is, one moment at a time, always going for what it is most likely to catch right then. It works up to a point, since each reply catches something useful. But the bucket stays empty. In the Introduction chapter, I mentioned a case how AI and a human would handle a situation differently. When sorting a customer complaint, and refering to how Bob did it, human asked Who's bob? AI would start a crusde to find him, his employement record etc, while a human would simply he was quite a few years before you - all you need is he is not current - and proceed with the complaint handling, the goal at hand.

[P4] A frequent example: after an introduction at a meeting, the model drafted the follow-up email. It wrote out our address, the road name and the year the mill was built, and never said why we wanted to meet.

[P5] Sometimes the butterfly is a puzzle. A prospective customer replied to one of our emails, and the model noticed that the email gave two different numbers for the same thing. It spent the rest of the session working out why, and the customer, who was the reason for the email, was forgotten. Asked why, the model said the numbers did not match, so it checked them.

[P6] The first pillar is to play for the goal.

Score each sentence on the nine offences below. A score is roughly how many intended readers in ten would meet the problem at that sentence (0 = none, 9 = nearly all).

1. Forgotten beat: for a paragraph's last sentence, score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to be left waiting for something this sentence opens which the next paragraph does not take up.
2. Unanchored reference: score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to have to search at this sentence for what a word (a name, "we", "this", a term) refers to.
3. Missing link: score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to have to work out alone how this sentence connects to the one before.
4. Out of order: score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to be confused at this sentence because it relies on something the text only gives later.
5. Repetition: score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to feel at this sentence that they are being told something they were already told.
6. Contradiction: score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to feel at this sentence that it conflicts with something earlier.
7. Purpose unclear: score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to have expected this sentence to deliver a point, find that it does not, and take that as a fault in the writing rather than a deliberate setup.
8. Register shift: score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to be jarred by a change of voice at this sentence that the text has not prepared; a sentence that announces a story is about to start counts as preparation.
9. Long dependency: score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to have to hold words in mind at this sentence because the words that belong together sit far apart.

Spelling and grammar do not count.

Write a TSV and nothing else. One row per sentence where any offence scores 2 or more, in reading order: paragraph.sentence (e.g. 3.2), TAB, the nine scores comma-separated in the order above, TAB, why: what the reader meets at this sentence, in at most 15 words except as the special instruction below requires. Describe the stumble, not a way to fix it. Last line: END.

Special instruction for the why field. Where contradiction (6) scores 5 or more, the why field must also say whether the conflict is real or only apparent, and why you think so. If it is apparent, quote the words that create it, say how they mislead, and say that the point itself holds. If it is real, name the two claims that cannot both be true. Leave any new wording to the writer. This changes the text you write, not the score: score what the reader feels, whatever your diagnosis.

1.why: Reader expecting the first pillar meets a personal kindergarten memory instead.

8.why: "Most likely to catch" sits oddly with a kitten chasing uncatchable butterflies.

9.why: "Each reply catches something useful" jars with the story's kitten achieving nothing.

10.why: Apparent: "catches something useful" then empty bucket; catch means momentary gain, bucket means goal; point holds. Bucket never in story.

11.why: Reader is told the Introduction's case again; link to the empty bucket unstated.

12.why: Who asks "Who's Bob?" and who answers is unclear; long tangled clauses retell the intro.

14.why: "A frequent example" of what is unstated after the Bob case.

15.why: "Our address", "the mill", "we" point to a business never introduced.

18.why: Reader holds "the customer" across an inserted relative clause before "was forgotten".

19.why: "Why" could mean either question; the model's excuse awaits a reply that never comes.

20.why: Sports phrase "play for the goal" closes a fishing story, and repeats the intro's pillar.

7.why: "But" sets AI against children who forget, yet both fail the lesson.

8.why: The kitten chased butterflies it rarely caught, not "what it is most likely to catch."

9.why: "Each reply catches something useful," but the story's kitten caught nothing at all.

10.why: "The bucket" never appeared in the story, and "stays empty" clashes with catching something useful. The conflict is apparent. "Catches something useful" in 3.4 suggests the catch is fish, so the reader expects the bucket to fill. The intended catch is the per-reply butterfly, which is not fish. The point holds: useful single replies do not add up to progress on the task.

11.why: A jump from the fishing metaphor to a cross-reference about the Introduction.

12.why: The reader must recall who Bob is and why a human asks about him.

13.why: "You" has no referent, and a dashed aside splits "would simply" from its sense. A human asked "Who's Bob?" in 3.7, yet here "a human" answers. The conflict is apparent. The bare word "human" names both the newcomer who asks and the experienced colleague who would answer, so they read as one person. The point holds: the AI and an experienced human are two alternative responders to the same question.

14.why: "A frequent example" of what? The link back to the kitten or Bob is unstated.

15.why: "Our," "we" and "the mill" are unexplained, and the reader must map address details to butterflies.

16.why: The reader must infer that the address details were the previous "butterfly."

17.why: "The email": is it ours or the customer's reply with two numbers?

18.why: "The email" is still ambiguous, and an inserted clause splits "the customer" from "was forgotten."

19.why: The model's excuse is quoted but not examined, and the next paragraph moves on.

20.why: The text shifts from fishing to a sporting image, and the pillar repeats the introduction.
